newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FEATURE - Sweden's IKEA sets its sights on China.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Sweden's IKEA sets its sights on China.

text.p: IKEA, Swedish home furnisher to the masses, is moving into China.
As the international household goods market shrinks, the world's biggest furniture retailer is targeting Asia.
In its home markets the low cost, no nonsense IKEA, has been forced to start cutting prices to support its market share and is looking eastwards to bolster sales.

Birger Ljung, outgoing managing director of IKEA retail in Sweden, said the group already had stores in Malaysia, Singapore, Taiwan and four in Hong Kong but from October this year he will spearhead a new drive into China.
"We are gradually moving east," Ljung, IKEA's new managing director for China, told Reuters.
"We have been in Asia for quite a while as a purchasing organisation but not in any great force as a retailer, being a European retailer of European origin.
"But the general idea is that if we can do business in other countries we can do business in China," said Ljung who will be based in Shanghai.
Since IKEA was set up in 1958 by Ingvar Kamprad, a farmer's son from Smaland in southern Sweden who is still chairman of the company, its success has been phenomenal.
Now with 130 self-service stores in 28 different countries, the IKEA group in the year to August 31, 1995, had a turnover of over $5 billion.
In 1995 it employed over 30,000 staff to sell its range of 11,400 products, some self-assembly, usually from out-of-town warehouses.
Germany was the company's biggest market in 1995, accounting for 29.9 percent of sales revenue, followed by Canada and the United States combined with 13.6 percent then Sweden with 10.6 percent.
"But the whole home decoration market has now been reduced," said Ljung who has been with IKEA for 18 years. "We want to improve our market position so we are growing out in a pretty aggressive way.
"We need to focus on China as longterm -- maybe Japan and Korea as well -- as this part of the world's growing in every way.

"We already have some contacts in China as we do some buying there but the main idea is that we'll design the products then go out to the market and find manufacturers to work for us and sell from there."
He said he was not yet sure if IKEA would jointly or wholly own its production facitilies. No date has yet been set for the opening of the first Chinese store and no sales targets set.
Ljung said it was unlikely IKEA would introduce a new range especially for the Chinese market with 95 percent of its stock the same the world over.
Its latest range, PS, launched last month, is characterised by block colours and rounded shapes in natural wood and chrome, inspired by the 1960s and 1970s.
Ljung said the organisation and products of IKEA, which now has its international headquarters in Denmark, reflects the down-to-earth attitude of founder, 69-year-old Kamprad.
"Functional objects for flatter not fatter wallets," is one of Kamprad's much quoted mottos.
Now living in Lausanne, Switzerland, Kamprad remains known for his thriftiness.
He made headlines in Swedish newspapers in 1992 when it was revealed that his claim for travel expenses to attend an interview at a Swedish television station showed he had taken a bus to the studio.

Although he has three sons, Kamprad in 1980 handed the ownership of IKEA over to a Dutch charitable foundation, Stichting Ingka, so the company could never be the victim of a hostile takeover or split up after his death.
He has, however, reportedly left his sons Habitat, the British-French "lifestyle" shop set up by designer Sir Terence Conran, which IKEA bought four years ago for 78 million pounds.
Kamprad's reputation came under a cloud in late 1994 when a Stockholm newspaper found his name in archives of the pro-Nazi activist Per Engdahl with whom he was friendly in the 1950s.
Kamprad wrote a letter of apology to all his employees, saying he was naive and young at the time when he admired Engdahl's anti-communist view, and he now bitterly regretted these links.
"I did not link them at all with Nazism. Only some years later did I understand that it was a big mistake," he said in the letter, referring to his action as "youthful sins".
